Test automation · Self-healing locators

Why UI tests break when nothing is broken

A renamed ID can stop a whole automation flow. This guide walks through the problem, the self-healing approach that solves it and how the matching works under the hood, with the open-source tool Healenium as the working example.

01The problem: one renamed ID breaks the flow

A developer renames one ID, login-btn becomes signin-btn, and the automation flow breaks. The button is still right there and nothing is actually wrong.

This is one of the most common ways UI automation fails without a real bug. Tests find elements through locators, locators depend on how a page is built, and pages change all the time.

Why it keeps happening

  • Developers rename IDs and classes while refactoring.
  • A UI library upgrade reshapes the page structure.
  • Frameworks generate IDs and class names that change between builds.
  • Third-party pages, like a payment checkout or a “Sign in with Google” popup, change on someone else’s schedule.

What it costs

  • Time: someone has to find the broken locator and fix it in every test that uses it.
  • Noise: red builds that are not real bugs.
  • Trust: after enough false alarms, people re-run or ignore failures, and real bugs slip through.

“But don’t developers tell testers before changing the UI?”

Often they do. But not every change is a deliberate rename. A UI library upgrade can reshape the page, and frameworks can regenerate IDs and class names on every build. A developer also can’t warn you about a locator they don’t know your tests use. And when your tests run through a third-party web app, the team that owns it changes elements on its own schedule and has no reason to tell outside testers.

Even when developers warn you in advance, someone still has to find and update that locator in every test that uses it. Until then, the automated test runs keep failing.

02Why locators are fragile

A Selenium test can’t see the page the way you do. It finds every element through a locator, such as an ID, a CSS selector or an XPath.

driver.find_element(By.ID, "login-btn").click()
Before the release
Test asks for #login-btn→Page has id="login-btn"→✓ Found, test continues
After the release
Test asks for #login-btn→Page has id="signin-btn"→✗ NoSuchElementException

Selenium doesn’t know the button got a new name. It only knows the old name no longer exists, so the test stops.

03The solution: self-healing locators

Instead of failing at the first broken locator, a self-healing layer gives the test a second chance. It works in four moves:

1

Remember

Save a fingerprint of each element every time a locator works.

2

Compare

When a locator breaks, compare the fingerprint with every element on the page.

3

Heal

Use the best match above a minimum score and keep the test running.

4

Log

Record the change so a person can review it and fix the code.

Several tools offer this. Healenium is a free, open-source option for Selenium, and it is the one used in the rest of this guide.

Animated explainer. A test clicks a Login button by its ID and passes, and Healenium saves a fingerprint of the button. A developer renames the ID and wraps the button in a new box, so the test fails. Healenium compares routes with LCS, compares details, scores every element and picks the Login button. The test keeps running and the heal is logged for review.

04How the matching works: trees and LCS

Two ideas do the heavy lifting. The page is treated as a tree, so every element has a route from the top of the page down to it. Routes are then compared with LCS, the Longest Common Subsequence algorithm. Step through it:

Animated walkthrough. The saved page and the new page are shown as trees. The saved route to the Login button is html, body, form, button. After the release it is html, body, form, div, button. An LCS table is filled cell by cell and returns 4, so all saved steps are found in order and the div is skipped. The Create account button also scores 4 of 4 on route, so details break the tie: the Login button matches 3 of 4 details and wins with the higher final score.

How the matching works: tree + LCS
Part 1 of 3 · The page is a tree
Saved (last passing run)
Now (after the release)
A web page is a tree of elements. On a passing run, Healenium saved the route to the Login button.
0:00

LCS in one paragraph

LCS finds the longest list of items two sequences share in the same order, even when other items sit in between. For the saved route html › body › form › button and the new route html › body › form › div › button, the answer is 4: every saved step is still there, and the extra div is skipped. It is a classic dynamic-programming problem, the same idea behind diff tools, and its cost grows with the two route lengths multiplied together.

Is it AI?

Not the way most people use the word today. Open-source Healenium uses no trained model and no LLM. It is a deterministic algorithm, tree comparison with LCS plus weighted similarity scoring, so the same page always gives the same answer.

05Where it fits: the architecture

What is hlm-proxy?

hlm is short for Healenium. hlm-proxy is a small program that runs on the test machine, between your test and Chrome. Your test sends every command to it, it passes each one on and it watches the answers. When an answer says “element not found”, it heals before your test ever sees the error.

Think of an office receptionist. You ask for extension 214. If that extension changed, the receptionist finds the person by name and connects you anyway.

The setup: many laptops, one shared server

Each laptop

Test, proxy and a real Chrome

The test, its own hlm-proxy and Chrome all run on the laptop, so a video call keeps using the laptop’s own network, microphone and camera.

One server

Memory and locator builder

Shared by every laptop. A fingerprint saved by one laptop can heal the same locator on the others.

Laptops only ever connect to the server, never the other way round. So you can add a laptop, or a laptop can change its IP address, without touching the server. The call’s audio and video never pass through the server; they go straight from each laptop’s Chrome to the meeting.

Architecture animation. Three laptops each run a test, a Healenium proxy and a real Chrome. One shared server holds the memory and the locator builder. On a normal run on Laptop 1, the test asks the proxy for the Login button, the proxy passes the request to Chrome, which finds it, and the proxy saves the button's fingerprint in the shared memory. On a healing run, Chrome cannot find the renamed button, so the proxy fetches the saved fingerprint, compares it with the page, asks the locator builder for a new locator, retries in Chrome, hands the button to the test and logs the heal.

The pieces

hlm-proxy:8085

On each laptop. The middleman: passes commands to Chrome, catches “not found” and runs the healing.

Chrome and ChromeDriver

On each laptop, as today. ChromeDriver is the small program Selenium already uses to control Chrome.

Memory:7878

On the server. hlm-backend with PostgreSQL: stores fingerprints and heals for all laptops, and serves the report.

Locator builder:8000

On the server. selector-imitator: turns the healed element into a ready-to-use locator.

Two ways to plug it in

Any language

Healenium-Proxy

Point your test’s driver at the proxy. Works with Python, Java, JavaScript and C#, with no other change to your tests.

Java only

Healenium-Web

Wrap your driver in code with SelfHealingDriver. No proxy needed.

06Quick setup with Python

1. On the server, once. Healenium’s own Compose file starts the memory and the locator builder. Open ports 7878 and 8000 to the laptops.

server
git clone https://github.com/healenium/healenium.git
cd healenium
docker-compose -f docker-compose-web.yaml up -d

2. On each laptop, once. Install Java 21 and download hlm-proxy-2.2.1.jar from the healenium-proxy releases page. Put it in the same folder as your tests.

3. Add the helper next to your tests. healenium_driver.py starts everything Healenium needs on the laptop, so there is nothing to start by hand:

  • Starts hlm-proxy if it isn’t running yet, and leaves it running for later tests.
  • Starts ChromeDriver on a fixed port for each test, and stops it when the test calls quit().
  • Falls back to plain Chrome if Java, the jar or the server is missing, so a test never fails because of Healenium.
healenium_driver.py
"""Create a Chrome driver, through Healenium when a server is given.

Save this file next to your tests and call
create_driver(options, hlm_server=...) where you used to call
webdriver.Chrome(options=options). Pass the server that runs Healenium's
memory and locator builder, for example from a --hlm-server option.

With hlm_server=None, or if any Healenium piece is missing, this returns a
plain webdriver.Chrome, so a test run never fails because of Healenium.

Optional environment variables (rarely needed):
    HLM_PROXY_JAR   path to hlm-proxy-2.2.1.jar (default: next to this file)
    HLM_JAVA        java command to use (default: java)
    SCORE_CAP       how close a match must be to heal (proxy default 0.6)
"""
import logging
import os
import socket
import subprocess
import time

from selenium import webdriver

PROXY_PORT = 8085  # hlm-proxy on this laptop
DRIVER_PORT = 9515  # ChromeDriver on this laptop
PROXY_START_TIMEOUT = 90  # seconds; the proxy is a Java app and starts slowly


def _is_listening(port):
    with socket.socket() as sock:
        sock.settimeout(1)
        return sock.connect_ex(("127.0.0.1", port)) == 0


def _ensure_proxy(hlm_server, log):
    """Start hlm-proxy if it is not running yet. It stays up for later runs."""
    if _is_listening(PROXY_PORT):
        return
    jar = os.environ.get(
        "HLM_PROXY_JAR",
        os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "hlm-proxy-2.2.1.jar"),
    )
    if not os.path.isfile(jar):
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"hlm-proxy jar not found: {jar}")
    env = dict(
        os.environ,
        SELENIUM_SERVER_URL=f"http://localhost:{DRIVER_PORT}",
        HEALENIUM_SERVICE=f"http://{hlm_server}:7878",
        IMITATE_SERVICE=f"http://{hlm_server}:8000",
    )
    log.info(f"Starting hlm-proxy from {jar}")
    subprocess.Popen(
        [os.environ.get("HLM_JAVA", "java"), "-jar", jar],
        env=env,
        stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL,
        stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL,
        start_new_session=True,  # keep it running after this script ends
    )
    deadline = time.monotonic() + PROXY_START_TIMEOUT
    while not _is_listening(PROXY_PORT):
        if time.monotonic() > deadline:
            raise TimeoutError(f"hlm-proxy did not open port {PROXY_PORT}")
        time.sleep(1)


def _start_chromedriver(options):
    """Start ChromeDriver on a fixed port, the same way webdriver.Chrome does."""
    from selenium.webdriver.chrome.service import Service
    from selenium.webdriver.common.driver_finder import DriverFinder

    service = Service(port=DRIVER_PORT)
    try:
        service.path = DriverFinder(service, options).get_driver_path()  # Selenium 4.20+
    except TypeError:
        service.path = DriverFinder.get_path(service, options)  # Selenium 4.11 to 4.19
    service.start()
    return service


def create_driver(options, *, hlm_server=None, log=None):
    """Return a Chrome driver: through Healenium when hlm_server is given."""
    log = log or logging.getLogger(__name__)
    if not hlm_server:
        return webdriver.Chrome(options=options)

    service = None
    try:
        _ensure_proxy(hlm_server, log)
        # ChromeDriver starts from this script, as before, so Chrome keeps the
        # same user, display and download folder.
        service = _start_chromedriver(options)
        driver = webdriver.Remote(
            command_executor=f"http://localhost:{PROXY_PORT}", options=options
        )
    except Exception:
        log.warning("Healenium not available, starting plain Chrome", exc_info=True)
        if service:
            service.stop()
        return webdriver.Chrome(options=options)

    plain_quit = driver.quit

    def quit_and_stop_chromedriver():
        try:
            plain_quit()
        finally:
            service.stop()

    driver.quit = quit_and_stop_chromedriver
    log.info(f"Chrome started through Healenium (server {hlm_server})")
    return driver

4. In your test, create the driver with the helper. Call it instead of webdriver.Chrome, and add a --hlm-server option to switch Healenium on. Here is a small sample test:

test_login.py
import argparse

from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By

from healenium_driver import create_driver

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--hlm-server", help="Healenium server; leave out to run without Healenium")
args = parser.parse_args()

options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
options.add_argument("--use-fake-ui-for-media-stream")  # auto-allow mic and camera for video calls

driver = create_driver(options, hlm_server=args.hlm_server)  # was: webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
try:
    driver.get("https://your-app.example/login")
    driver.find_element(By.ID, "login-btn").click()
finally:
    driver.quit()

The --use-fake-ui-for-media-stream flag only skips the permission prompt; the call still uses the real microphone and camera. Don’t add --use-fake-device-for-media-stream, which swaps them for a test pattern.

5. Run your tests. Pass --hlm-server to turn Healenium on. Leave it out and the same test runs with plain Chrome, as before.

terminal
# Healenium on
python test_login.py --hlm-server hl-server

# Healenium off: plain Chrome, as before
python test_login.py

The same commands work on Windows, macOS and Linux. Replace hl-server with your server’s IP address or hostname. Every heal is recorded in the report at http://hl-server:7878/healenium/report.

Alternative: manual setup without the helper

If you’d rather not add the helper, start the two pieces yourself on each laptop before the tests: ChromeDriver on a fixed port in one terminal, and the proxy in another, with three addresses.

terminal
# ChromeDriver on this laptop, on a fixed port
chromedriver --port=9515

# hlm-proxy: where ChromeDriver is, and where the server is
SELENIUM_SERVER_URL=http://localhost:9515 \
HEALENIUM_SERVICE=http://hl-server:7878 \
IMITATE_SERVICE=http://hl-server:8000 \
java -jar hlm-proxy-2.2.1.jar

Then point the driver at the proxy on the same laptop:

python
driver = webdriver.Remote(
    command_executor="http://localhost:8085",  # hlm-proxy on this laptop
    options=options,
)

Using Java instead? Add the healenium-web dependency and wrap your driver with SelfHealingDriver.create(driver).

07What it heals and how to use it safely

What it heals

  • Renamed IDs, classes and other attributes
  • Small layout shifts: an extra wrapper box, a moved element, a broken absolute XPath

Use it safely

  • Treat a healed pass as a warning, not a clean pass.
  • Review the report after each run and update the locator in your code.
  • Turn healing off for release gates, where you want strict results.
  • Keep stable test IDs (data-testid) as your first line of defence.
  • Find elements with find_element rather than inside JavaScript strings, so Healenium can heal them.
  • If you see a wrong heal, raise the minimum match (score-cap).

Cost: the open-source version is free under the Apache 2.0 license. A paid Pro edition on AWS Marketplace adds AI-suggested fixes as GitHub pull requests and Playwright support. For most Selenium teams, open source is enough.

08Wrap-up

The problemA small UI change breaks the automation flow even when nothing is wrong, and every fix costs time and trust.
The solutionSelf-healing locators remember each element, find it again with tree and LCS matching, keep the test running and log the change for review.

Healenium is one practical way to get there with Selenium today. Pair it with stable test IDs and a habit of reviewing every heal, and a red build starts meaning a real bug again.
